doctrines.name: The Holy Spirit and the Gifts
doctrines.question: Does the Holy Spirit still give miraculous gifts, and how do believers receive the Spirit?
doctrines.summary: All Christians confess the Holy Spirit as "Lord and Giver of Life". They differ sharply over whether prophecy, tongues and healing continue, whether Spirit-baptism is a second experience evidenced by tongues, and who may speak with prophetic or apostolic authority, from the Montanist crisis to Pentecostalism, the charismatic renewal and today’s prosperity and apostolic movements.
doctrines.longText:
The New Testament presents the Spirit as the gift of the last days: poured out at Pentecost with tongues and prophecy, distributing gifts "to every man severally as he will" (1 Cor 12:11), and producing love, joy and peace. Second-century writers such as Justin and Irenaeus describe prophecy and healing in their churches as a matter of course. But the New Prophecy of Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla in Phrygia (from c.156), with its ecstatic first-person oracles and claim to the Paraclete’s final discipline, forced the Church to decide how prophecy relates to apostolic tradition. The first recorded synods rejected it, and suspicion of ecstatic prophecy deepened.

In the 4th century the focus shifted to the Spirit’s divinity, confessed at Constantinople (381) as "the Lord and Giver of Life ... who spake by the prophets". Chrysostom and the young Augustine observed that the Corinthian gifts no longer occurred, though Augustine later recorded many healings. Eastern Christianity never developed a doctrine of cessation: holy elders, wonder-working saints and mystics such as Symeon the New Theologian kept alive an expectation of conscious experience of the Spirit. In the West, miracles were associated with saints and relics, and the Reformers, confronting both Catholic miracle claims and radical "enthusiasts", argued that the gospel needed no new miracles: the seed of Protestant cessationism, systematised by B. B. Warfield in 1918.

Wesleyan teaching on a second work of grace and the 19th-century Holiness movement prepared the ground for Pentecostalism. In 1901 Charles Parham taught that tongues were the evidence of Spirit-baptism; from 1906 the Azusa Street revival led by William J. Seymour sent missionaries worldwide, alongside parallel revivals in Wales, India, Korea and Chile. From 1960 the charismatic renewal brought Pentecostal experience into Anglican, Lutheran and Catholic churches; the 1980s "Third Wave" brought it to evangelicals; and since the 1970s the Word of Faith and prosperity teachings and the New Apostolic Reformation have generated intense controversy.

Today Pentecostal and charismatic Christians number perhaps 600–650 million, concentrated in Africa, Latin America and Asia. The debates (cessationism versus continuationism, initial evidence, the testing of prophecy, prosperity and apostolic authority) are among the most practically consequential in world Christianity, shaping worship, healing ministry, mission and even politics. This section sets out each view in the words its adherents would recognise before giving its critics’ objections.

nodes.label: Does the Holy Spirit still give miraculous gifts, and how do believers receive the Spirit?
nodes.text: Pentecost poured out the Spirit with tongues, prophecy and healings. Did these gifts cease with the apostles, or continue? Is there a distinct "baptism in the Spirit" after conversion, and is it evidenced by tongues? Who may speak in the Spirit’s name today, and how is prophecy tested?

nodes.label: Joel 2:28–32 and Acts 2: "I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh"
nodes.text: Peter interprets Pentecost’s tongues as Joel’s promise for "the last days" and "to all that are afar off" (Acts 2:39). Pentecostals read Acts 2, 8, 10 and 19 as a pattern; others as unrepeatable salvation-historical firsts.

nodes.label: John 14–16: the Paraclete who will guide into all truth
nodes.text: Jesus promises "another Comforter" who will teach and "guide you into all truth" (John 16:13). Montanists and Joachites claimed new Paraclete revelation; the wider Church insisted the Spirit witnesses to Christ and does not add to the apostolic faith.

nodes.label: 1 Corinthians 12–14: varieties of gifts, one Spirit
nodes.text: Paul lists wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discernment, tongues and interpretation (12:8–10), asks "do all speak with tongues?" (12:30), and says prophecies and tongues will cease "when that which is perfect is come" (13:8–10), which cessationists have read as the completed canon or apostolic era, and continuationists as Christ’s return.

nodes.label: Irenaeus: brethren in the Church prophesy and speak in tongues
nodes.text: Irenaeus treats prophecy, tongues and even raising the dead as continuing in the catholic Church of his day, against Gnostic claims to secret gifts.

nodes.label: The New Prophecy (Montanism)
nodes.text: In Phrygia, Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla speak ecstatically in the first person as the Paraclete, call for stricter fasting and readiness for martyrdom, and point to Pepuza as the New Jerusalem.

nodes.label: Objection: ecstatic, first-person prophecy breaks with tradition
nodes.text: Anonymous and Apollonius (in Eusebius) and Miltiades argue that true prophets do not speak in ecstasy or frenzy, that the prophetesses left their husbands and took gifts, and that their predictions failed.

nodes.label: Asian synods excommunicate the New Prophecy (c.177)
nodes.text: The first recorded church synods in Asia Minor examine and reject the New Prophecy; Rome, after hesitation, follows (c.200). Montanist communities survive in Phrygia until Justinian’s persecution in the 6th century.

nodes.label: Tertullian joins the New Prophecy (c.207)
nodes.text: The Carthaginian theologian embraces the Paraclete’s new discipline (no remarriage, stricter fasting, no flight in persecution), while remaining orthodox on the Trinity.

nodes.label: Basil and Constantinople 381: the Spirit is "Lord and Giver of Life"
nodes.text: The debate shifts from gifts to the Spirit’s person: Basil defends worship of the Spirit "with" the Father and Son; the Creed of 381 confesses the Spirit "who spake by the prophets".

nodes.label: Chrysostom and Augustine: the signs "were adapted to the time"
nodes.text: Late-4th-century fathers observe that the Corinthian gifts no longer occur in their churches and treat tongues as a sign for the Church’s founding era.

nodes.label: Augustine revises: "even now miracles are wrought"
nodes.text: In City of God 22.8 Augustine catalogues healings in Hippo and corrects his earlier view, a passage both sides cite.

nodes.label: Symeon the New Theologian: conscious experience of the Spirit
nodes.text: The Byzantine mystic insists that baptism in the Spirit must be consciously experienced, often with tears and vision of divine light, an Eastern current later valued by charismatics. Eastern Orthodoxy never formally adopted cessationism; miracles of saints and holy elders remain expected.

nodes.label: Luther against the "heavenly prophets" (1522–25)
nodes.text: Confronted by the Zwickau prophets and Karlstadt, Luther insists the Spirit comes through the external Word and sacraments, not apart from them. Reformers counter Catholic appeals to miracles by arguing that new miracles are unnecessary to confirm an old gospel.

nodes.label: Cessationism
nodes.text: B. B. Warfield’s Counterfeit Miracles (1918) systematises Reformation instincts: sign-gifts authenticated the apostles and ceased with them and the closed canon.

nodes.label: Wesley: the gifts waned because love grew cold
nodes.text: Wesley’s theology of a second work of grace (entire sanctification) became, through the Holiness movement, the template for a post-conversion "baptism in the Spirit".

nodes.label: Pentecostal initial evidence
nodes.text: At Bethel Bible School, Topeka, Agnes Ozman speaks in tongues on 1 January 1901; Charles Parham teaches tongues as the "Bible evidence" of Spirit baptism.

nodes.label: Azusa Street revival (1906–09)
nodes.text: Under the African American preacher William J. Seymour, a multiracial revival in Los Angeles sends missionaries worldwide; parallel outpourings occur in Wales (1904), India (Mukti, 1905), Korea (Pyongyang, 1907) and Chile (Valparaíso, 1909).

nodes.label: Assemblies of God fixes "initial physical evidence" (1916)
nodes.text: The AG Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916) makes tongues the initial physical sign of Spirit baptism, a doctrinal boundary for classical Pentecostalism; some Pentecostals (e.g. the Chilean Methodist Pentecostal Church) never adopted it.

nodes.label: Continuationism
nodes.text: All the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 remain available until Christ returns, though not tied to a second experience or to tongues as evidence; represented in Grudem’s Four Views (1996).

nodes.label: Charismatic renewal in the historic churches
nodes.text: Dennis Bennett, an Episcopal rector in Van Nuys, announces he has spoken in tongues (1960); renewal spreads to Lutherans, Anglicans and, from the Duquesne weekend (1967), Catholics.

nodes.label: Rome welcomes the Catholic Charismatic Renewal (1975)
nodes.text: Paul VI addresses 10,000 charismatics in St Peter’s at Pentecost 1975, calling the renewal a "chance for the Church"; Cardinal Suenens’ Malines Documents (1974) interpret "baptism in the Spirit" as a release of sacramental grace. Later popes, including Francis (CHARIS, 2019), affirm it.

nodes.label: The Third Wave
nodes.text: John Wimber and C. Peter Wagner’s Fuller course MC510 (1982) and the Vineyard: signs and wonders for ordinary evangelicals, without a second-blessing theology.

nodes.label: Vineyard and the Toronto Blessing (1994–95)
nodes.text: Holy laughter and other manifestations at the Toronto Airport Vineyard draw hundreds of thousands; in December 1995 the Association of Vineyard Churches withdraws its endorsement over concerns about the focus on manifestations.

nodes.label: Word of Faith and the prosperity gospel
nodes.text: Kenneth Hagin’s Rhema Bible Training Center (1974), Kenneth Copeland and Oral Roberts’ "seed faith" teach that faith-filled confession secures health and wealth; exported to Africa, Latin America and Asia.

nodes.label: New Apostolic Reformation
nodes.text: Wagner’s networks of contemporary apostles and prophets, the "Seven Mountains" mandate, strategic-level spiritual warfare.

nodes.label: Objections: Lausanne, Pentecostal scholars and NAR critics
nodes.text: The Lausanne Cape Town Commitment (2010) rejects the excesses of the prosperity gospel as contrary to biblical teaching on suffering, generosity and the poor; Pentecostal scholars such as Gordon Fee had already called health-and-wealth teaching a "disease" (1985); critics of the NAR (Geivett and Pivec, 2014) challenge governing apostles and failed prophecies, e.g. about the 2020 US election.

nodes.label: Pentecostalisation of global Christianity
nodes.text: Pentecostal, charismatic and independent Spirit-movements grow from a few million in 1910 to hundreds of millions, above all in Africa, Latin America and Asia (Yoido Full Gospel Church, Seoul; Redeemed Christian Church of God, Nigeria; Brazilian Assemblies of God), reshaping worship, healing ministry and social mobility.

nodes.label: Today: a Spirit-shaped world Christianity
nodes.text: The World Christian Database counts roughly 600–650 million Pentecostals and charismatics (c.2020), about a quarter of all Christians. Cessationism remains strong in confessional Reformed and some Baptist circles (e.g. Strange Fire conference, 2013); most evangelical scholars are "open but cautious" continuationists; Catholic and Orthodox churches acknowledge charisms within sacramental order. Fresh revivals (Asbury, 2023) and debates over prophecy, prosperity and apostolic authority continue.

nodes.label: Asbury outpouring (2023)
nodes.text: A chapel service at a Wesleyan-Holiness university in Kentucky extends into two weeks of continuous worship, notable for its deliberate lack of celebrity leadership and manifestations, illustrating a quieter, Holiness-style expectation of the Spirit.

positions.name: Montanism (the New Prophecy)
positions.oneLine: The promised Paraclete was speaking afresh through the prophets Montanus, Priscilla and Maximilla, calling the Church to stricter discipline and readiness for Christ’s coming.
coreClaims: The Paraclete promised in John 14–16 now speaks directly through new prophets, completing the revelation of discipline (not of doctrine).
Prophecy may come in ecstasy, with the prophet speaking in the first person as God.
Christians should fast more strictly, refuse second marriage and not flee persecution.
The heavenly Jerusalem would descend at Pepuza in Phrygia.
Women may be prophets and, in later Montanist communities, hold clerical office.
keyTexts: Tertullian, On Monogamy; On Fasting; On Flight in Persecution
positions.origin: Began in Phrygia (central Asia Minor) around 156–172 (sources differ) when the recent convert Montanus began prophesying ecstatically at Ardabau, joined by Priscilla (Prisca) and Maximilla. It spread to Rome, Gaul and North Africa, where Tertullian embraced it c.207. Its own name was "the New Prophecy".
proponentsOther: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity is often thought to reflect New Prophecy sympathies (debated)
strongestArguments: The New Testament promises continuing prophecy until Christ’s return (Acts 2:17; 1 Cor 13:8–12), and the second-century Church still had prophets (Didache 11; Irenaeus).
Its morality was rigorous and its doctrine of God orthodox; Tertullian’s Trinitarian theology was written as a Montanist.
It resisted the growing domestication of the Spirit by bishops and the laxity of a settling Church.
It recognised women’s prophetic ministry in line with Acts 2 and 21:9.
strongestObjections: Ecstatic, first-person speech "as God" broke with the tradition of prophets who spoke in their right mind (1 Cor 14:32: "the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets").
Its prophecies failed: Maximilla predicted wars and the end after her death, yet there was a long peace (Anonymous in Eusebius 5.16.19).
By claiming the Paraclete’s final revelation it relativised the apostolic deposit and implied a new authority above the bishops and Scripture.
Critics accused its leaders of financial exploitation and of encouraging needless martyrdom.
responses: Montanists replied that the Paraclete added discipline, not doctrine, and that the "rule of faith" was unchanged (Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins 1).
Modern historians (Trevett, Tabbernee) argue that much early polemic was exaggerated, and that the movement was largely a conservative, rigorist renewal of older Asian prophetic Christianity.
consequences: Prompted the first recorded church synods (Asia Minor, c.177) and helped push the Church towards a closed canon and episcopal control of prophecy.
Contributed to suspicion of ecstatic prophecy and of women’s leadership in the catholic Church.
Survived in Phrygia until suppressed by Justinian in the 6th century; John of Ephesus burned the relics of the founders at Pepuza (c.550).
Became a perennial reference point: cessationists see it as the archetype of charismatic excess, while some Pentecostals see it as an unjustly suppressed renewal.

positions.name: Cessationism
positions.oneLine: The miraculous or "sign" gifts (prophecy, tongues, healings, miracles) were given to authenticate the apostles and complete Scripture, and ceased with the apostolic age.
coreClaims: Miraculous gifts functioned chiefly to authenticate new revelation and its messengers (2 Cor 12:12; Heb 2:3–4).
The apostles and prophets were the once-for-all foundation of the Church (Eph 2:20); with the canon complete, revelatory gifts are no longer needed.
Biblical miracles cluster around epochs of revelation (Moses, Elijah/Elisha, Christ and the apostles) rather than occurring evenly.
God still answers prayer and may heal providentially, but no one today possesses the gift of healing or infallible prophecy.
"Ordinary" gifts (teaching, service, giving, leadership) continue.
positions.origin: Patristic observations that the gifts had become rare (Chrysostom, Augustine’s early writings) were turned into a doctrine by Reformation polemic against Catholic miracle claims and radical "enthusiasts": Calvin argued that new miracles were not needed to confirm the old gospel (Prefatory Address to the Institutes, 1536). John Owen and the Puritans developed it, and B. B. Warfield’s Counterfeit Miracles (1918) gave the classic modern statement in reaction to faith-healing and early Pentecostalism.
strongestArguments: It protects the sufficiency and finality of Scripture: if prophecy continues, new revelation competes with the canon.
The New Testament itself presents apostolic signs as distinctive credentials ("the signs of an apostle", 2 Cor 12:12), not as universal equipment.
Modern tongues and prophecy, it argues, differ from the New Testament phenomena (known languages in Acts 2; infallible prophecy in the Old Testament standard of Deut 18).
Church history shows a marked decline of claimed sign-gifts after the apostolic era, and recurrent movements claiming them have often produced error and abuse.
strongestObjections: No text explicitly says the gifts will cease before Christ returns; most commentators read "that which is perfect" (1 Cor 13:10) as the eschaton, when we see "face to face".
Patristic sources (Justin, Irenaeus, Tertullian, and Augustine’s own later City of God 22.8) report continuing miracles; the decline was gradual and contested (Ruthven).
It fits poorly with widespread reports of healings and prophetic experience in the Global South, where most Christians now live.
Paul commands "forbid not to speak with tongues" and "desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy" (1 Cor 14:1, 39) without time limits.
responses: Cessationists reply that 1 Corinthians 13 is not their main argument; the foundational, authenticating role of the gifts is.
Many distinguish their view ("the sign gifts ceased") from denying miracles: God remains free to heal in answer to prayer.
They argue that the quality of modern phenomena, not their quantity, is decisive, and that much reported prophecy is fallible impression rather than New Testament prophecy.
consequences: Shaped the worship and expectations of most confessional Reformed and many Baptist and fundamentalist churches.
Fuelled early fundamentalist hostility to Pentecostalism (e.g. the World’s Christian Fundamentals Association’s 1928 resolution against it).
Continues in vigorous debate with continuationists in global evangelicalism (Strange Fire conference, 2013).

positions.name: Continuationism
positions.oneLine: All the gifts of the Spirit, including prophecy, tongues and healing, remain available to the Church until Christ returns, to be exercised in love and tested by Scripture.
coreClaims: The gifts are for "the common good" (1 Cor 12:7) and the building up of the Church in every age, not merely for authenticating apostles.
They will cease only "when that which is perfect is come", i.e. at Christ’s return (1 Cor 13:10–12).
New Testament prophecy is distinct from canonical Scripture and must be weighed (1 Thess 5:19–21; 1 Cor 14:29).
Spirit baptism normally occurs at conversion; tongues are one gift among many, not required evidence.
positions.origin: The working assumption of the 2nd-century Church (Justin, Irenaeus) and never formally abandoned in Eastern Orthodoxy or Catholicism, where charisms and miracles of saints remain expected. Within Protestantism it was revived through Wesleyan, Holiness and Pentecostal currents and given academic articulation by evangelical scholars such as Wayne Grudem (The Gift of Prophecy, 1988), Gordon Fee and D. A. Carson (Showing the Spirit, 1987).
strongestArguments: It takes the New Testament’s instructions on gifts as addressed to the whole Church, not only to the first generation.
The burden of proof lies on cessationism, since no text explicitly limits the gifts to the apostolic era.
It coheres with documented miracle reports across history and today (Craig Keener’s two-volume survey, 2011).
It fosters expectant prayer and ministry in line with Jesus’ commission to heal and cast out demons.
strongestObjections: Cessationists argue that "fallible prophecy" is a novel category that undermines the seriousness of claiming "thus says the Lord".
Critics point to abuses, false prophecies and manipulative healing campaigns within continuationist movements.
Some argue that contemporary tongues are learned speech patterns rather than languages (linguistic studies, e.g. William Samarin, 1972).
responses: Continuationists reply that abuse of a gift calls for discernment, not prohibition (1 Thess 5:20–21).
They argue that New Testament congregational prophecy was always subject to weighing and was never treated as canonical (1 Cor 14:29; Acts 21:4, 10–14).
Paul calls some tongues "tongues of angels" (1 Cor 13:1) and treats them as prayer not necessarily in human languages (1 Cor 14:2, 14).
consequences: Allowed charismatic practice within Reformed and Baptist churches (e.g. Sovereign Grace Churches, New Frontiers).
Became the majority stance among evangelical scholars and most Global South churches.
Lowered barriers between evangelicals and Pentecostals/charismatics.

positions.name: Pentecostal initial evidence
altNames: Baptism in the Holy Spirit with the evidence of tongues
positions.oneLine: Baptism in the Holy Spirit is an experience distinct from and subsequent to conversion, empowering for witness, whose initial physical evidence is speaking in tongues.
coreClaims: Every believer should seek the baptism in the Holy Spirit as promised in Acts 1:5–8 and 2:38–39.
This baptism is distinct from, and normally subsequent to, regeneration.
Its initial physical evidence is speaking in other tongues as the Spirit gives utterance (Acts 2:4; 10:46; 19:6).
Its purpose is power for witness and service, not salvation.
All the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12 are for today.
positions.origin: Building on Wesleyan and Holiness teaching on a "second blessing" and on Reformed "higher life" Spirit-baptism (Keswick, R. A. Torrey), Charles F. Parham at Bethel Bible School in Topeka, Kansas, concluded that tongues were the biblical evidence; Agnes Ozman spoke in tongues on 1 January 1901. William J. Seymour carried the teaching to Azusa Street, Los Angeles (1906). The Assemblies of God enshrined "initial physical evidence" in its Statement of Fundamental Truths (1916).
strongestArguments: In Acts, whenever the outpouring of the Spirit is described in detail (Acts 2, 10, 19), tongues accompany it, and in Acts 10:46 tongues is how Peter’s companions knew the Spirit had been given.
Acts 8 and 19 show believers who had received Christ but not yet the Spirit’s empowering, supporting subsequence.
It provides a clear, objective sign that encourages believers to seek empowerment, and its fruit is visible in the extraordinary missionary expansion of Pentecostalism.
strongestObjections: Paul’s rhetorical question "do all speak with tongues?" expects the answer no (1 Cor 12:30).
Narrative texts in Acts describe what happened, not necessarily what must always happen; Acts 8 mentions no tongues.
Paul says all believers were baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Cor 12:13), suggesting Spirit-baptism is conversion-initiation (James Dunn, Baptism in the Holy Spirit, 1970).
Even Seymour later came to regard tongues alone as an insufficient evidence, stressing love; many Pentecostals in Chile, Germany and elsewhere never accepted the doctrine.
responses: Pentecostals distinguish the "gift of tongues" for public ministry (not all have it, 1 Cor 12:30) from the "sign of tongues" accompanying Spirit baptism (available to all).
They argue that Luke is a theologian in his own right whose narratives teach a distinct pneumatology of empowerment (Roger Stronstad, 1984), not merely Paul’s soteriology.
Contemporary Pentecostal theologians (Macchia) reframe tongues as a sacramental sign of the Spirit’s presence rather than a mechanical test.
consequences: Became the defining doctrine of classical Pentecostal denominations (Assemblies of God, Church of God, Pentecostal Holiness Church, Foursquare).
Drew a sharp line between Pentecostals and both Holiness churches and fundamentalists, who largely rejected the movement.
Contributed to the Oneness ("New Issue") split of 1916 and later debates within charismatic renewal about whether tongues are necessary.
Fuelled vigorous mission in Africa, Latin America and Asia.

positions.name: Charismatic renewal
positions.oneLine: Pentecostal-style experience of the Spirit and the gifts, embraced within the historic denominations without leaving them and usually without the initial-evidence doctrine.
coreClaims: The baptism or "release" of the Spirit renews faith, worship and mission within existing churches.
All the gifts, including tongues, prophecy and healing, are available today.
Tongues are common but not required as evidence.
Renewal should serve the unity and sacramental life of the Church rather than create new denominations.
In Catholic and Anglican interpretation, "baptism in the Spirit" actualises grace already given in baptism and confirmation.
positions.origin: In 1960 Dennis Bennett, rector of St Mark’s Episcopal Church, Van Nuys, California, told his congregation he had spoken in tongues, and the renewal spread through Episcopalians, Lutherans (Larry Christenson), Presbyterians, Baptists and, after a retreat at Duquesne University in February 1967, Roman Catholics. Michael Harper’s Fountain Trust (1964) spread it in Britain. Cardinal Suenens’ Malines Documents (1974) and Paul VI’s address of 1975 gave Catholic recognition.
strongestArguments: It brings renewed devotion, Scripture reading and evangelism to people who remain in sacramental and liturgical churches, demonstrating that charisms and institutions need not compete.
It has strong ecumenical fruit, bringing Catholics and Protestants together in prayer and worship.
Patristic and liturgical sources (Kilian McDonnell and George Montague, Christian Initiation and Baptism in the Holy Spirit, 1991) suggest that charisms were originally part of Christian initiation.
strongestObjections: Critics fear it creates a two-tier membership of "Spirit-filled" and ordinary Christians, dividing congregations.
Cessationists and some confessional Lutherans see it as importing subjective experience over Word and sacrament.
Some Pentecostals regard its rejection of initial evidence and its tolerance of Catholic doctrine (e.g. Marian devotion) as compromise.
responses: Charismatic leaders insist that all baptised Christians have the Spirit and that renewal is about releasing what is already given, not a superior class.
Church authorities have provided pastoral oversight (e.g. Catholic National Service Committees; Anglican guidelines) to keep renewal integrated with parish life.
consequences: The Catholic Charismatic Renewal is estimated to have touched well over 100 million Catholics, especially in Latin America, Africa and the Philippines (El Shaddai).
Transformed Protestant worship through "contemporary worship" music.
Helped spawn independent charismatic churches and networks when renewal was rejected locally.
Created new ecumenical bridges (e.g. Catholic–Pentecostal dialogue since 1972).

positions.name: Third Wave
altNames: Third Wave of the Holy Spirit
positions.oneLine: Evangelicals can expect "signs and wonders" (healing, prophecy, deliverance) as part of normal kingdom ministry without adopting Pentecostal second-blessing doctrine or labels.
coreClaims: Spirit baptism occurs at conversion; subsequent "fillings" empower ministry.
Healing, words of knowledge and deliverance are normal tools of evangelism ("power evangelism").
Kingdom theology: the kingdom has already broken in (Ladd), so signs of it should accompany preaching.
Every believer can "do the stuff" Jesus did, not only specially gifted leaders.
positions.origin: The term was coined by C. Peter Wagner of Fuller Theological Seminary (1983) for a "third wave" after Pentecostalism and the charismatic renewal. John Wimber, a former Quaker musician and church-growth consultant, taught the course MC510 "Signs, Wonders and Church Growth" at Fuller (1982) and led the Association of Vineyard Churches.
strongestArguments: It integrates spiritual gifts with mainstream evangelical theology rather than requiring a two-stage experience.
Missionary anthropologists (Kraft) argue that in many cultures "power encounters" are central to conversion, as in the New Testament.
Its kingdom framework is rooted in respected biblical scholarship (Ladd).
strongestObjections: Critics argue that its claimed healings were seldom medically verified and that pragmatic church-growth logic drove it.
The Kansas City Prophets controversy (1990) and Toronto Blessing (1994) raised questions about discernment and manifestations.
Cessationists and some Pentecostals say it blurs biblical distinctions while adopting charismatic practice.
responses: Wimber publicly admitted mistakes (e.g. with the Kansas City Prophets) and the Vineyard disassociated from Toronto in 1995, showing willingness to self-correct.
Advocates point to the evangelistic fruit and humility-focused "naturally supernatural" ministry style.
consequences: Vineyard worship music shaped global evangelical worship.
Brought charismatic practice into many evangelical churches without Pentecostal labels.
Wagner’s later work led into the New Apostolic Reformation.

positions.name: New Apostolic Reformation (NAR)
positions.oneLine: God is restoring the offices of apostle and prophet to govern the Church and lead it to transform society, in what C. Peter Wagner called a "Second Apostolic Age".
coreClaims: The five-fold ministry of Ephesians 4:11 (apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, teachers) continues, including governing apostles.
Apostles lead relational networks rather than denominations; prophets receive revelation for strategy.
Strategic-level spiritual warfare against territorial spirits advances the kingdom.
Many adherents embrace a "Seven Mountains Mandate" to influence family, religion, education, media, arts and entertainment, business and government.
A coming great harvest and transformation of nations are prophesied.
positions.origin: Named by C. Peter Wagner in the mid-1990s (popularised in Churchquake!, 1999), building on the Latter Rain movement (1948), Third Wave and the global rise of independent apostolic networks, especially in Africa, Latin America and Asia. Wagner founded the International Coalition of Apostles (1999) and dated the "Second Apostolic Age" from 2001. The Seven Mountains idea is traced to Loren Cunningham and Bill Bright (1975) and was developed by Lance Wallnau and Johnny Enlow.
proponentsOther: Bill Johnson (Bethel Church; rejects the label)
strongestArguments: Ephesians 4:11–13 gives the five ministries "till we all come in the unity of the faith", implying they continue until maturity is reached.
Network-based apostolic leadership fits rapidly growing churches in the Global South better than inherited denominations.
It recovers a vision of the gospel transforming every sphere of life, not only private piety.
strongestObjections: Most traditions hold that apostles in the foundational sense (witnesses of the risen Christ, Acts 1:21–22; 1 Cor 15:8) were unrepeatable, laid once as the Church’s foundation (Eph 2:20).
Critics (Geivett and Pivec, 2014) charge it with authoritarianism, lack of accountability and new extra-biblical revelation.

Seven Mountains and dominion theology are criticised as a form of Christian nationalism, and prominent prophets’ failed predictions (e.g. Donald Trump’s re-election in 2020) damaged credibility; some, like Jeremiah Johnson, publicly apologised.
Pentecostal denominations, including the Assemblies of God (2000 position paper on apostles and prophets), warn against its claims.
responses: Advocates distinguish the twelve foundational apostles from ongoing "functional" apostles who plant and oversee churches, a sense used for Barnabas and others (Acts 14:14).
Leaders such as Bill Johnson disown the NAR label and the most authoritarian forms; adherents say it is a loose, diverse network, not a single organisation.
consequences: Shaped large independent charismatic networks globally and much of charismatic political activism in the US and Brazil.
Contributed to the "prophetic" politics of the 2016–2024 US elections and the January 2021 Capitol rally rhetoric, prompting sharp critique from fellow charismatics.
Spurred renewed debate on apostolic authority and prophetic accountability.

positions.name: Word of Faith and the prosperity gospel
positions.oneLine: Through Christ’s atonement believers are entitled to health and material blessing, which they appropriate by faith-filled confession and generous giving.
coreClaims: Christ bore sickness and poverty as well as sin (Isa 53:4–5; 2 Cor 8:9), so healing and prosperity are covenant rights.
Words spoken in faith release spiritual power ("positive confession"); negative words can bind.
Giving is sowing a "seed" that God multiplies back (seed-faith).
God wills believers to prosper and be in health (3 John 2; Deut 8:18).
In stronger forms, believers are "little gods" restored to Adamic authority (contested within the movement).
positions.origin: E. W. Kenyon (1867–1948), influenced by Holiness, Higher Life and (critics argue) New Thought ideas, taught the authority of the believer and positive confession; Kenneth Hagin popularised Kenyon’s ideas (Rhema Bible Training Center, 1974). Oral Roberts’ "seed faith" (from 1950s), Kenneth Copeland, Fred Price, Benny Hinn and Creflo Dollar extended it through television. It spread worldwide: David Yonggi Cho’s "threefold blessing" (Korea), Edir Macedo’s Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (Brazil, 1977), David Oyedepo’s Living Faith Church Worldwide (Nigeria, 1981).
strongestArguments: Scripture does promise material blessing to God’s people and presents God as generous (Deut 28; Mal 3:10; Phil 4:19), which much Western theology neglects.
Salvation in the Bible is holistic (shalom), including body and circumstances, which resonates with the poor in the Global South.
Sociologists (e.g. David Martin, Miller and Yamamori) note that it can foster sobriety, saving, education and entrepreneurship that lift families out of poverty.
strongestObjections: Jesus and the apostles taught suffering, self-denial and contentment, warning against the love of money (Mark 8:34; 1 Tim 6:5–10; Phil 4:11–13); Paul himself was often poor and sick (2 Cor 11:27; Gal 4:13).
The Lausanne Cape Town Commitment (2010) and many Pentecostal scholars (Gordon Fee, 1985) reject it as a distortion of the gospel that exploits the poor and blames the sick for weak faith.

Critics such as D. R. McConnell (1988) trace Kenyon’s teaching to metaphysical New Thought rather than Pentecostal roots, and question its "little gods" anthropology and claims that Jesus was "born again" in hell.
High-profile scandals, luxury lifestyles and fundraising abuses have damaged its credibility.
responses: Advocates reply that poverty is a curse Christ came to break, and that critics write from affluent contexts.
Many "soft prosperity" teachers repudiate extreme claims and stress generosity, stewardship and hope rather than guarantees.
Some Global South theologians argue for a "gospel of empowerment" that keeps prosperity’s holistic concern while rejecting manipulation.
consequences: Became one of the most widespread forms of popular Christianity in Africa, Latin America and parts of Asia, and in US megachurches.
Prompted vigorous critique from evangelicals, Pentecostal denominations, Catholic bishops and African theologians.
Influenced American political-religious culture (e.g. spiritual advisers to presidents) and media religion.

controversies.question: Can new prophecy add to the apostolic faith?
controversies.title: The New Prophecy (Montanist) controversy
controversies.summary: In 2nd-century Phrygia, Montanus and the prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla claimed the Paraclete was speaking through them with new disciplines and an imminent end. The resulting conflict produced the first recorded church synods and helped define how the Church tests prophecy and relates it to Scripture and bishops.

sides.name: The New Prophecy
sides.steelman: Christ promised the Paraclete would lead us into all truth. The same Spirit who spoke through Agabus and Philip’s daughters now speaks through our prophets, not to change the faith but to call a lax Church to the discipline and courage the last days require. The bishops who silence the Spirit are quenching what Paul told us not to quench.
arguments: Moral seriousness and readiness for martyrdom
counterArguments: Ecstatic first-person prophecy differs from biblical prophecy

sides.name: Catholic bishops and apologists
sides.steelman: We do not despise prophecy; Irenaeus rejoices that brothers in the Church prophesy. But true prophets speak with self-control, agree with the apostolic rule of faith, and are tested by the whole Church. A prophecy that claims to be the Paraclete himself, abandons sober speech, makes predictions that fail and sets itself above the apostolic tradition is not from the Spirit of Christ.
arguments: Spirits of prophets are subject to prophets (1 Cor 14:32)
counterArguments: Risk of quenching the Spirit and institutionalising the Church

timeline.text: Montanus begins prophesying at Ardabau in Phrygia (date per Epiphanius; Eusebius suggests c.172).
Synods in Asia Minor examine and excommunicate the New Prophecy; the martyrs of Lyon write to Rome counselling peace.
After initial sympathy, Roman bishops reject the New Prophecy.
Tertullian in Carthage embraces the New Prophecy.
Tertullian’s Against Praxeas accuses Praxeas of driving out the Paraclete at Rome.
Under Justinian, John of Ephesus destroys the Montanist shrine and relics at Pepuza.

resolution.text: The catholic Church excommunicated the New Prophecy, which survived as a separate church in Phrygia and North Africa (Tertullianists) until the 6th century. The episode strengthened episcopal authority, the closing of the canon and caution toward ecstatic prophecy.

consequences: First recorded church synods held to settle a doctrinal question.
Contributed to the sense that revelation ended with the apostles and to the formation of the New Testament canon.
Set a pattern of suspicion toward ecstatic prophecy and female prophetic leadership.

controversies.question: Are the miraculous gifts of the Spirit for today?
controversies.title: Cessationism versus continuationism
controversies.summary: Do prophecy, tongues, healing and miracles continue in the Church, or did they cease with the apostles? The question, sharpened by the Reformation and then by the rise of Pentecostalism, divides evangelicals and shapes worship, mission and pastoral practice worldwide.

sides.name: Cessationist
sides.steelman: The sign-gifts were the credentials of the apostles and the scaffolding of a Church still receiving revelation. Once the foundation was laid and Scripture completed, the scaffolding came down. God still heals in answer to prayer, but to claim ongoing prophecy is to threaten the sufficiency of Scripture, and history shows how often such claims lead people astray.
counterArguments: No text sets an end-date before Christ’s return
Augustine and others reported continuing miracles

sides.name: Continuationist (open but cautious)
sides.steelman: Paul told the Corinthians to desire spiritual gifts and not to forbid tongues, and said these gifts would end only when we see Christ face to face. Prophecy today is not Scripture: it is weighed and tested. The Church should neither despise prophecy nor believe every spirit.
arguments: Gifts are for the common good of every church
Patristic and modern reports of miracles
counterArguments: Category of fallible prophecy is novel

sides.name: Pentecostal (initial evidence)
sides.steelman: The promise is "to you and to your children and to all that are afar off". Pentecost was not a one-off but the pattern: believers are baptised in the Spirit for power to witness, and the Bible evidence is speaking in tongues. The explosive growth of Spirit-filled churches across the world is the Lord confirming the word with signs following.

timeline.text: Pentecost: tongues and prophecy at the Church’s birth.
The New Prophecy controversy raises the question of continuing prophecy.
Chrysostom notes that the Corinthian gifts no longer occur.
Augustine records contemporary healings (City of God 22.8).
Calvin argues that new miracles are not needed to confirm the gospel.
Welsh revival heightens expectation of a new Pentecost.
Azusa Street revival launches global Pentecostalism.
Warfield’s Counterfeit Miracles.
Charismatic renewal reaches the historic denominations.
Toronto Blessing provokes fierce debate over manifestations.
Grudem’s Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views.
John MacArthur’s Strange Fire conference attacks the charismatic movement; widespread continuationist rebuttals follow.
Asbury revival reopens discussion of revival without manifestations.

resolution.text: Unresolved. Pentecostal, charismatic and most Global South churches are continuationist; Catholic and Orthodox churches affirm charisms within sacramental order; confessional Reformed and some Baptist churches remain cessationist; many evangelical networks treat the question as secondary.

consequences: Defines denominational boundaries and church-planting networks.
Shapes worship style, healing ministry and deliverance practice worldwide.
Drives a large apologetic and scholarly literature on miracles.

controversies.question: Does faith guarantee health and wealth, and are there apostles and prophets today?
controversies.title: Prosperity gospel and the New Apostolic Reformation
controversies.summary: Since the 1970s, two influential streams within independent charismatic Christianity, the Word of Faith/prosperity gospel and the New Apostolic Reformation, have provoked strong criticism from evangelicals, Pentecostal denominations and Catholic bishops, while flourishing in the Global South and in American media.

sides.name: Word of Faith / prosperity teachers
sides.steelman: Christ became poor that we might become rich, and by his stripes we were healed. God is not glorified by his children living in sickness and lack. When believers speak God’s promises in faith and sow generously, they reap the blessing the covenant guarantees, and that message is good news to the world’s poor.
counterArguments: Suffering and contentment in the New Testament

sides.name: New Apostolic Reformation
sides.steelman: Christ gave apostles and prophets as well as pastors and teachers until the Church reaches maturity. God is again raising apostolic leaders to equip the saints and prophets to give direction, so that the Church can disciple whole nations and every sphere of society.

sides.name: Critics (evangelical, Pentecostal, Catholic)
sides.steelman: The Spirit’s gifts are real, but the gospel is the message of the cross, not a technique for wealth, and the apostles’ foundational authority is not transferable. The Lausanne Movement, Pentecostal scholars and many African theologians warn that these movements exploit the poor, silence accountability and confuse the kingdom of God with worldly success or political power.
arguments: Love of money is a root of evil (1 Tim 6:10)
counterArguments: Critics may ignore real social uplift and holistic blessing

timeline.text: Kenneth Hagin opens Rhema Bible Training Center in Tulsa.
Edir Macedo founds the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God in Rio de Janeiro.
Pentecostal scholar Gordon Fee publishes The Disease of the Health and Wealth Gospels.
D. R. McConnell’s A Different Gospel traces the Faith movement to E. W. Kenyon.
C. Peter Wagner’s Churchquake! and the International Coalition of Apostles.
The Lausanne Cape Town Commitment rejects the excesses of the prosperity gospel.
Several charismatic prophets apologise for failed prophecies about the 2020 US election.

resolution.text: No central authority governs these networks. Critique continues from Lausanne, Pentecostal denominations and Catholic bishops, while both movements remain widespread, particularly in Africa, Latin America and US media.

consequences: Shaped popular Christianity in many Global South countries.
Linked charismatic Christianity with political mobilisation in the US and Brazil.
Provoked internal reform movements and greater emphasis on prophetic accountability.

people.name: B. B. Warfield
people.summary: Benjamin Breckinridge Warfield, the leading Old Princeton theologian, defended biblical inerrancy (with A. A. Hodge, 1881) and Calvinist orthodoxy. His Counterfeit Miracles (1918) gave cessationism its classic modern statement: the miraculous gifts authenticated the apostles and ceased with them. He held a postmillennial eschatology and, unusually for his circle, accepted that evolution could be compatible with Scripture.

works.title: Against Praxeas
works.summary: Tertullian’s refutation of the modalist Praxeas, written after he had embraced the New Prophecy.
works.significance: First Latin use of "trinitas" in a developed sense; also a Montanist-era polemic accusing Praxeas of driving out the Paraclete.

works.title: On the Holy Spirit (De Spiritu Sancto)
works.summary: Basil’s defence of the full divinity of the Spirit and of the doxology "with the Spirit", against the Pneumatomachi.
works.significance: Prepared the way for the confession of the Spirit as "Lord and Giver of Life" at Constantinople (381); key source for unwritten apostolic tradition.

works.title: Homilies on First Corinthians
works.summary: Forty-four homilies preached at Antioch on 1 Corinthians.
works.significance: Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians 12 records that the charismata described by Paul no longer occurred in Chrysostom’s day, a text later cited by cessationists.

works.title: Homilies (Tractates) on the First Epistle of John
works.summary: Ten Easter-season sermons on love in 1 John.
works.significance: Contains the classic "signs adapted to the time" passage on tongues (6.10) and the saying "love, and do what you will" (7.8).

works.title: Counterfeit Miracles
works.summary: Warfield’s Thomas Smyth lectures (Columbia Seminary, 1917) surveying patristic, medieval, Irvingite, faith-healing and Christian Science miracle claims.
works.significance: The classic statement of modern Protestant cessationism.

works.title: The More Excellent Way (Sermon 89)
works.summary: Wesley’s sermon on 1 Corinthians 12:31 contrasting extraordinary gifts with the "more excellent way" of love.
works.significance: Argues the extraordinary gifts declined because love grew cold after Constantine, not because God withdrew them: an early non-cessationist reading influential on Holiness and Pentecostal movements.

works.title: The Apostolic Faith (Los Angeles)
works.summary: Newspaper published from the Azusa Street Mission, edited by William J. Seymour and Clara Lum (1906–08), reaching tens of thousands of readers worldwide.
works.significance: Spread news of the Azusa Street revival and Pentecostal doctrine globally.

works.title: Power Evangelism
works.summary: John Wimber (with Kevin Springer) on evangelism accompanied by healing, deliverance and words of knowledge as signs of the kingdom.
works.significance: Manifesto of the "Third Wave", drawing on George Ladd’s kingdom theology.

works.title: Churchquake! How the New Apostolic Reformation Is Shaking Up the Church As We Know It
works.summary: C. Peter Wagner’s account of networks led by contemporary apostles and prophets.
works.significance: Named and promoted the New Apostolic Reformation.

quotes.text: In like manner we do also hear many brethren in the Church, who possess prophetic gifts, and who through the Spirit speak all kinds of languages, and bring to light for the general benefit the hidden things of men, and declare the mysteries of God.

In an oracle preserved by Epiphanius, the Spirit speaking through Montanus says that a human being is like a lyre and the Spirit like the plectrum that strikes it: the man sleeps while the Spirit keeps watch.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of a Montanist oracle in Epiphanius, Panarion 48.4.1 (c.377)

quotes.text: He became beside himself, and being suddenly in a sort of frenzy and ecstasy, he raved, and began to babble and utter strange things, prophesying in a manner contrary to the constant custom of the Church handed down by tradition from the beginning.
quotes.citation: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.16.7 (NPNF 2nd ser. vol. 1, tr. McGiffert), quoting an anonymous anti-Montanist writer on Montanus

quotes.text: Praxeas did a twofold service for the devil at Rome: he drove away prophecy, and he brought in heresy; he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father.
Through the Holy Spirit comes our restoration to paradise, our ascension into the kingdom of heaven, our return to the adoption of sons.
quotes.citation: Basil of Caesarea, On the Holy Spirit 15.36 (NPNF 2nd ser. vol. 8)

quotes.text: This whole place is very obscure: but the obscurity is produced by our ignorance of the facts referred to and by their cessation, being such as then used to occur but now no longer take place.
quotes.citation: John Chrysostom, Homilies on 1 Corinthians 29.1, on 1 Cor 12:1–2 (NPNF 1st ser. vol. 12)

quotes.text: In the earliest times, the Holy Ghost fell upon them that believed: and they spake with tongues, which they had not learned, as the Spirit gave them utterance. These were signs adapted to the time.
quotes.citation: Augustine, Homilies on the First Epistle of John 6.10 (NPNF 1st ser. vol. 7)

quotes.text: For even now miracles are wrought in the name of Christ, whether by His sacraments or by the prayers or relics of His saints.
quotes.citation: Augustine, City of God 22.8 (NPNF 1st ser. vol. 2, tr. Dods)

quotes.text: The real cause was, "the love of many," almost of all Christians, so called, was "waxed cold."
quotes.citation: John Wesley, Sermon 89, "The More Excellent Way" (1787), §2, on why the extraordinary gifts became rare after Constantine

quotes.text: These gifts were not the possession of the primitive Christian as such; nor for that matter of the Apostolic Church or the Apostolic age for themselves; they were distinctively the authentication of the Apostles.
quotes.citation: B. B. Warfield, Counterfeit Miracles (New York: Scribner, 1918), lecture 1, p. 6

quotes.text: Pentecost Has Come: Los Angeles Being Visited by a Revival of Bible Salvation and Pentecost as Recorded in the Book of Acts
quotes.citation: The Apostolic Faith (Los Angeles) vol. 1 no. 1 (September 1906), front-page headline

quotes.text: Parham taught his Topeka students that speaking in tongues was the biblical evidence of the baptism in the Holy Spirit, and at first believed the tongues would be real foreign languages that would let missionaries preach without learning them.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Charles F. Parham, A Voice Crying in the Wilderness (1902), and accounts of Bethel Bible School, January 1901

quotes.text: Wimber argued that the gospel advances most powerfully when proclamation is accompanied by demonstrations of God’s power, such as healing and deliverance, which break down resistance and reveal that the kingdom of God has arrived.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of John Wimber and Kevin Springer, Power Evangelism (1986), chs. 2–3

quotes.text: Wagner claimed that around 2001 the Church entered a "Second Apostolic Age", in which recognised apostles and prophets once again govern networks of churches and give strategic direction for transforming society.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of C. Peter Wagner, Churchquake! (1999) and Apostles Today (2006)

quotes.text: Hagin taught that believers, by speaking in faith what God has promised in Scripture, can appropriate healing and material provision that are already theirs through Christ’s redemption; doubt and negative confession block the blessing.
quotes.citation: Paraphrase of Kenneth E. Hagin, How to Write Your Own Ticket with God (1979) and other Rhema teachings
